Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

issues.item: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Hard to Recall Deliberately' conflicts with 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.' Deliberate retrieval difficulty and very easy verbal access are opposing states and are hard to reconcile as describing the same patient at the same time, especially alongside 'Overwhelm on Recall,' which implies traumatic recall is effortful and dysregulating rather than easy to discuss.

issues.item: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' directly conflicts with 'When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop.' At this severity level and with strong Trigger↔Memory and Memory→Threat links, these two memory items describe opposing levels of accessibility/distress and are hard to reconcile as the same current presentation.

issues.item: Triggers: Authority Commands: Being given orders or instructions
issues.explanation: The trigger set is hard to reconcile with stalking as the index trauma: 'authority commands' and especially 'bicycle' do not show an evident clinical link to the reported trauma, and the profile provides no memory or appraisal content that would make these idiosyncratic triggers understandable.

Threat items emphasize broad interpersonal attack and generic danger vigilance (loud sounds, scanning exits, watching others for harm), which fits assault/combat/fire trauma better than stalking. For stalking, one would expect threat focused more on being followed, approached, monitored, contacted, or found by the perpetrator.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: 'I am a weak person' sits awkwardly with this profile and occupation unless supported by appraisal content about failure to protect oneself or family; here the other appraisals center on permanent damage and fear of going crazy, so the weakness item feels less coherent with the stalking-specific formulation than those items.

vignette:
The stalking began with small things that Amir could almost explain away. A bicycle that appeared too often on his route home from the firehouse. The same sedan parked a few houses down from his own, engine idling, then gone by the time he looked again. He was a firefighter-he was trained to assess threats, to stay calm under pressure. For weeks he told himself he was being paranoid. But then the notes started appearing under his windshield wiper, and the calls came at odd hours, and the bicycle began to show up outside the station itself, always just far enough away that he could never get a good look at the rider. The night it finally broke-the night he came home to find the back door unlocked and a single photograph of his wife on the kitchen counter, a photograph he had never seen before-he called the police, filed a report, and spent the next three months sleeping with a crowbar under his pillow. The stalker was never caught. The case went cold. And Amir, who had spent his entire adult life running into burning buildings, found himself unable to walk to his own mailbox without his heart slamming against his ribs.

That was fourteen months ago. Now, sitting in a therapist's office for the first time, Amir cannot bring himself to say the word "stalking" out loud. He knows what happened-he can see the photograph, the curve of the kitchen counter, the exact shade of dusk coming through the window-but when he tries to describe it, the words jam somewhere in his throat. He gestures, shakes his head, and finally says, "I can't. I just can't." It is not that he has forgotten. It is that remembering feels like being dropped into the middle of that night all over again, and the emotion that floods him-terror, rage, a kind of sick helplessness-is so overwhelming that he has to stop talking, close his eyes, and breathe until his hands stop shaking. The memories do not come when he expects them. A car door slamming in the parking lot of the grocery store can drop him straight back into that kitchen. The squeak of bicycle brakes on the street outside the firehouse can make him freeze mid-sentence, his coffee cup halfway to his lips, his entire body locked in a moment that is over but somehow never ends.

Amir has changed, and he knows it. He used to be the guy who cracked jokes in the engine bay, the one who could walk into any burning apartment and immediately map the layout, the exits, the points of collapse. Now he does the same thing in every room he enters, but not for the reasons he used to. He scans for exits because he is certain that someone is watching him, that someone might come through a door he has not accounted for. He watches strangers in restaurants, in the firehouse lobby, at his son's school pickup, cataloguing their hands, their eyes, the angle of their bodies-looking for the tell that means they intend to harm him. Loud, unexpected sounds make him flinch so hard that his colleagues have started to notice. He has told them he is just tired. He is not tired. He is terrified that he is losing his mind. The way his body reacts before his brain can catch up, the way he cannot stop checking the back seat of his car even when he knows no one is there-these things feel to Amir like evidence that something inside him has broken permanently. He used to believe he was strong. He ran into buildings when everyone else ran out. Now he believes that the stalking did not just scare him; it revealed that he was never strong in the first place. A strong person would have moved on by now. A strong person would not be jumping at bicycle bells and scanning parking lots like a hunted animal.

The avoidance has reshaped his life in ways he did not anticipate. He stopped riding his bicycle-the one he used to take to work on sunny days-because the sight of another bike on the road made his stomach drop. He takes longer, more circuitous routes to the firehouse now, avoiding the blocks where he used to see the sedan. He has stopped going to the grocery store after dark. He has stopped walking his son to the bus stop in the morning. His wife has started doing all of these things alone, and she does not complain, but Amir sees the worry in her face, and he knows that she is carrying something that should be shared. He cannot bring himself to tell her the full truth about what he feels-that he is afraid all the time, that he thinks he might be going crazy, that he watches her sleep some nights because he is terrified that the stalker has found them again and he will not hear the door open. He has come to therapy because his captain pulled him aside after he froze during a call-a routine kitchen fire, nothing dangerous-and told him that he needed to get help or he would be put on leave. That scared Amir more than the stalking ever did. Losing his job would mean losing the one place where he still felt like himself, even if that self is fading. He is not sure he can get better. He is not sure he deserves to. But he showed up anyway, and that, at least, feels like the first thing he has done right in over a year.
